messages.subject: Side-by-side strip plots
messages.subject_clean: Side-by-side strip plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Inspired by Prof. Bryan Hanson's example the other day, I became curious as to how to dodge strip plots correctly in ggplot2.

# Manufactured data:

d <- data.frame(A = factor(rep(letters[1:3], each = 10)),
                B = factor(rep(rep(c(1, 2), each = 5), 3)),
                y = as.vector(mapply(rnorm, 5, c(5, 7, 10, 5, 12, 14))) )

I am looking to get strip plots for each level of factor A dodged by the levels of factor B, but my simplistic efforts have been in vain thus far.

# The initial basic plot:
g <- ggplot(d, aes(x = a, y = y, color = b, fill = b))
g + geom_point()

None of the following work wrt the desired outcome:

g + geom_point(position = 'dodge')           # Nothing changes
g + geom_point(position = 'dodge', width = 0.4)     # Ditto, but I expected this...
g + geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5))    # Not quite...

The same message appears at each invocation, associated with the position = argument:
ymax not defined: adjusting position using y instead

The last attempt makes some progress in the sense that the B groups align on either side of the A level, but the values are jittered rather than in a vertical strip.

The message confuses me in that I'm trying to adjust the x-position of the strip plots  :)  Moreover, the help page says that the arguments are width and height.

I've consulted the book and the archives of this group but haven't found out how to produce such a graph.

So the question is: how to get pairs of strip plots at each level of factor A?

TIA,
Dennis

messages.subject: how to override several scatter plots in the same coordinates
messages.subject_clean: how to override several scatter plots in the same coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggploters,

I need your kind helps on how to override several scatter plots in the
same coordinates. I have two objective variables ("a" and "b") and
their own backgrounds ("abackground","bbackground"). I want to plot
all these four variables in the same coordinates, with the background
ones in the lower layers in grey colors and the objective ones in the
upper layers in bright colors. I have tried following the clue of the
ggplot2 book. But, I am failed. Now, I ask for helps here.

Your helps are very valuable for me.

Thanks in advance.
####################################################
# generate my data set
x<-c(rnorm(n=50, mean=1, sd=2), rnorm(n=50, mean=10, sd=2),
rnorm(n=1000, mean=1, sd=3),rnorm(n=1000, mean=10, sd=3))
y<-c(rnorm(n=50, mean=1, sd=2), rnorm(n=50, mean=10, sd=2),
rnorm(n=1000, mean=1, sd=3),rnorm(n=1000, mean=10, sd=3))
gp<-c(rep(c("a","b"),each=c(50,50)),rep(c("abackground","bbackground"),
each=c(1000, 1000)))

mydata<-data.frame(gp, x, y)

####################################################
# ggploting

library(ggplot2)
#################################
# the first try.
pp<-ggplot(mydata, aes(y, x, group = gp)) + geom_point()
(pp + geom_point(aes(group="a"), se=4, fill="blue")) # does not work

################################
# the second try.
library(NCStat)
a.data<-Subset(mydata, gp=="a")
b.data<-Subset(mydata, gp=="b")
a.background<-Subset(mydata, gp=="abackground")
b.background<-Subset(mydata, gp=="bbackground")

(pp + geom_point(data=a.data,aes(y, x, color="honeydew3"))
	+ geom_point(data=b.data,aes(y, x, color="yellow4")
	+ geom_point(data=a.background,aes(y, x, color="cyan")
	+ geom_point(data=b.background,aes(y, x, color="blue")))

Best.

Mao Jian-Feng

messages.subject_clean: rxnNorm Demo
messages.body_plain:
Good Morning all... Several have asked for the code to make these plots, so the code and a test case that produces the attached plots are attached (thanks for the interest).

I collaborate with an ecologist and we are working on plant stress, studying different levels of stress and different genotypes of a plant.  In ecology they like to create plots like the ones shown to see if there is a genotype x stress effect, which is evidenced by non-parallel or crossing lines.  In these plots, the response is on the y axis, the stress (either categorical or numerical) is on the x axis, and the different sets of lines are the genotypes.  Of course, this could be adapted in a number of ways for similar purposes.

You’ll note that the boxplot option executes but doesn’t give quite what is expected.  If anyone sees what’s wrong with it, I’d love to know.  Everything else seems to work OK.

Also, the stat_summary functions I call are from my ChemoSpec package available at http://github.com/bryanhanson/ChemoSpec.  Any function you write that returns a measure of central tendency and two extremes will work, it just has to return 3 values to stat_summary.

Have fun.  Suggestions welcome.  Bryan
*************
Bryan Hanson
Acting Chair
Professor of Chemistry & Biochemistry
DePauw University, Greencastle IN USA

b.background<-subset(mydata, gp=="bbackground")

ggplot()+
geom_point(data=a.background,aes(x=x, y=y), color="grey70") +
geom_point(data=b.background,aes(x=x, y=y), color="grey50")+

geom_point(data=b.data,aes(x=x, y=y),  color="blue")

messages.subject: Passing arguments through ... with ggplot() functions: some make it, some don't
messages.subject_clean: Passing arguments through ... with ggplot() functions: some make it, some don't
messages.body_plain:
I thought I had this fixed...

The function I shared yesterday includes ... In the argument list.  Near the bottom of the function, the ... appear as an argument to opts().  If I put title = “test” into the function call, the title is correctly displayed.  If I put ylab = “test” it does not come through.  I suppose I am putting the ... in the wrong place.

Function and test data below.  I’m sure someone who has been doing functions using ggplot can find this quickly, but my various permutations don’t seem to work! Sorry the stuff below is so long.   Thanks, Bryan
*************
Bryan Hanson
Professor of Chemistry & Biochemistry
DePauw University, Greencastle IN USA

#### typical use:

p <- rxnNorm(data = td, res = "r", fac1 = "f1", method = "sem", freckles = TRUE, fac2cols = c("red", "green", "blue"), ylab = "something", type = "connect", title = "test", fac2 = "f2"); print(p)

##### test data:

res = c(rnorm(10, 5, 1.5), rnorm(10, 8, 2), rnorm(10, 14, 2.0), rnorm(10, 10, 1.5), rnorm(10, 15, 2), rnorm(10, 12,2.5))
fac1 <- c(rep("L", 20), rep("M", 20), rep("H", 20))
fac1 <- factor(fac1, levels = c("L", "M", "H"))
fac2 <- c(rep("WT", 10), rep("DOM", 10))
fac2 <- rep(fac2, 3)
fac2 <- as.factor(fac2)
num1 <- c(rep(5, 20), rep(10, 20), rep(12, 20))
junk <- rep(1,60) # to be thrown away later during data compression

td <- data.frame(r = res, f1 = fac1, f2 = fac2, no1 = num1, junk)
td[5, 3] <- NA # remove a few values here and there
td[30, 2] <- NA
td[37, 2] <- NA
td[47, 1] <- NA
td[18, 4] <- NA

rm(fac1) # clean up workspace
rm(fac2)
rm(junk)
rm(res)
rm(num1)
##### function:

rxnNorm <- function(data = NULL, res = NULL,
    fac1 = NULL, fac2 = NULL, fac2cols = NULL,
    freckles = FALSE, type = c("connect", "fitLine"),
    method = c("sem", "iqr", "mad", "box", "sem95"),
    table = NULL, ...) {

# Function to compare categorical data by
# plotting means etc in the same panel
# Option to connect the dots or do a fit
# Bryan Hanson, DePauw Univ, July 2010

# Both fac1 and fac2 must be given: this is G x E!
# fac2 must be a factor, but fac1 can be either factor or numeric
# Everything related to a particular level of fac2 should be colored the same

    require(ggplot2)
    require(ChemoSpec) # on GitHub
    require(plyr)
    require(ggExtra)

    if (is.null(fac2cols)) stop("You need to supply fac2cols")

    # 1st, reduce the df and clean it of NAs
    # otherwise there is trouble with the counts
    # plus this keeps the ggplot2 object size down

    keep <- c(res, fac1, fac2)
    data <- data[, keep]
    data <- na.omit(data)

    # Specify the data & aesthetics

    p <- ggplot(data, aes_string(x = fac1, y = res, color = fac2,
        group = fac2))

    # now add layers as requested

    if (freckles) {
        jit <- position_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.0)
        p <- p + geom_jitter(position = jit, size = 1.0)
        }

    if (method == "box") { # this doesn't work right
        p <- p + geom_boxplot(width = 0.2)
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "sem") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXy")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "sem95") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXy95")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "mad") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXyMad")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "iqr") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXyIqr")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (type == "fitLine") {
        p <- p + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

        }

    # now add the common decorations & modifications

    p <- p  + scale_colour_manual(name = "", values = fac2cols) +
        opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(colour = "black"),
        axis.text.y = theme_text(colour = "black"),
        axis.ticks = theme_blank()) + opts(...)

    # now add summary tables
    # using a nice table feature from ggExtra

    if (!is.null(table)) {

        if (type == "connect") {
            counts <- count(data, vars = c(fac2, fac1))
            colnames(counts) <- c(fac2, fac1, "count")

            p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = counts,
                theme = theme.list(show.box = TRUE, separator = "black",
                gp = gpar(cex = table[3]),
                   show.csep = TRUE, show.rsep = TRUE, show.colnames = TRUE,
                   show.rownames = FALSE))
            }

        if (type == "fitLine") {
            lvls <- levels(data[,fac2])
            nl <- length(lvls)
            m <- c()
            b <- c()
            r2 <- c()
            for (i in 1:nl) {
                dat <- subset(data, data[,fac2] == lvls[i])
                mod <- lm(dat[,res] ~ dat[,fac1])
                m[i] <- round(mod$coef[2], 2)
                b [i]<- round(mod$coef[1], 2)
                r2[i] <- round(cor(dat[,fac1], dat[,res])^2, 4)

                }

            mod.res <- data.frame(line = lvls, m = m, b = b, r2 = r2)

            p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = mod.res,
                theme = theme.list(show.box = TRUE, separator = "black",
                gp = gpar(cex = table[3]),
                   show.csep = TRUE, show.rsep = TRUE, show.colnames = TRUE,
                   show.rownames = FALSE))

            }
        }
    invisible(p)
    }

On Mon, Aug 2, 2010 at 11:17 AM, Christopher Moore <canoe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Brandon,
>
> Using "group=" and "groups=" doesn't appear to make a difference.  When the "linetype=" argument is not wrapped inside aes(), it results in an error:

This behavior is documented. When an aesthetic is set, it can only assume one value; when an aesthetic is mapped (i.e., inside an aes() statement), it can assume more than one value. In
p + geom_line(linetype=group)
linetype is set, but since group is a factor with multiple values, an inconsistency is found and the error is thrown. When you wrapped linetype inside an aes() statement, i.e.,

p + geom_line(aes(linetype=group)) #produces desired plot

linetype was mapped to the levels of group, so multiple linetypes were created and a legend was drawn.

As Hadley noted in the ggplot2 book (p. 47-48, section 4.5.2):
"Instead of mapping an aesthetic property to a variable, you can set it to a single value by specifying it in the layer parameters. Aesthetics can vary for each observation being plotted, while parameters do not. We *map* an aesthetic to a variable (e.g., aes(colour = cut)) or *set* it to a constant (e.g., colour = 'red'). ""

HTH,
Dennis

I simulated some data that reflect my real data.  It appears that group membership must remain static in order to vary line types.  The simulation below shows that if one stays in the same group (FRP.Flag) over time, then ggplot can handle different line types, but if one moves between groups over time, then only color variation can be used to represent group membership.  The downside of this is that color variation can get obscured when printing in grayscale.  Varying line types can help maintain fidelity when printing.

> "Instead of mapping an aesthetic property to a variable, you can set it to a single value by specifying it in the layer parameters. Aesthetics can vary for each observation being plotted, while parameters do not. We *map* an aesthetic to a variable (e.g., aes(colour = cut)) or *set* it to a constant (e.g., colour = 'red'). ""

>         }
>
>     if (method == "box") { # this doesn't work right

>         if (type == "connect") {
>             p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
>                 }
>         }
>

>

>

>         }
>

>
>         }
>
>     # now add the common decorations & modifications
>
>     p <- p  + scale_colour_manual(name = "", values = fac2cols) +
>         opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(colour = "black"),
>         axis.text.y = theme_text(colour = "black"),
>         axis.ticks = theme_blank()) + opts(...)
>
>     # now add summary tables
>     # using a nice table feature from ggExtra
>
>     if (!is.null(table)) {
>
>         if (type == "connect") {
>             counts <- count(data, vars = c(fac2, fac1))
>             colnames(counts) <- c(fac2, fac1, "count")
>
>             p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = counts,
>                 theme = theme.list(show.box = TRUE, separator = "black",

>                    show.rownames = FALSE))
>             }
>
>         if (type == "fitLine") {
>             lvls <- levels(data[,fac2])
>             nl <- length(lvls)
>             m <- c()
>             b <- c()
>             r2 <- c()
>             for (i in 1:nl) {
>                 dat <- subset(data, data[,fac2] == lvls[i])
>                 mod <- lm(dat[,res] ~ dat[,fac1])
>                 m[i] <- round(mod$coef[2], 2)
>                 b [i]<- round(mod$coef[1], 2)
>                 r2[i] <- round(cor(dat[,fac1], dat[,res])^2, 4)
>
>                 }
>
>             mod.res <- data.frame(line = lvls, m = m, b = b, r2 = r2)
>
>             p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = mod.res,

>                    show.csep = TRUE, show.rsep = TRUE, show.colnames = TRUE,

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

After reading this qqnorm and ggplot2 post (http://groups.google.com/
group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/e0dc61c51b1e992e), I was wondering
how to specify custom quantile in stat_qq. Any suggestion welcome!

Thank you in advance,

Thomas

On Jan 11, 4:59 pm, hadley wickham <h.wick...@gmail.com> wrote:
is what base-R does, not what ggplot actually does. It might be that
ggplot is right, I am not knowledgeable enough to know that, but I
think it should be justified on the help page of stat_qq, with an
appropriate reference. And, at least because it is different from the
default behaviour of R (however wrong it may be), it should be
strongly argumented.

Ok, I finally get what you're complaining about and I think you're
right - I was using the quantiles for both the sample and theoretical
distributions, when I should only be using them for the theoretical.

Here's what the new code will look like:

    data <- remove_missing(data, na.rm, "sample", name = "stat_qq")

    sample <- sort(data$sample)
    n <- length(sample)

    # Compute theoretical quantiles
    if (is.null(quantiles)) {
      quantiles <- ppoints(n)
    } else {
      stopifnot(length(quantiles) == n)
    }
    theoretical <- safe.call(distribution, list(p = quantiles, ...))

    data.frame(sample, theoretical)

But that means you can no longer specify (e.g.) quantiles = seq(0.05,
0.95, by = 0.05)) if you have a large dataset and only want to see
select quantiles.  I think that was my original intention, which I now
see is a bit different to qqnorm.

Hadley

Hi,

I looked for a while without success :(
Is it possible to bin values on the horizontal axis when using
stat_summary… This would allow much greater flexibility when
summarizing data will small jittering in x. I wondered if it would be
possible to use stat_bin but I doubt it is possible to call two stats
simultaneously. I'm probably missing something obvious…

Here is some small example to illustrate this point:

library(ggplot2)
d <- data.frame(a = rep(c(1,3,5), 10),
	b = rnorm(30),
	c = rep(1:10, each=3))

# works fine if points are aligned
qplot(a, b, data=d, color=factor(c), geom=c("point", "path")) +
stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal", geom = "errorbar", width=0.5,
colour="black")

# if the data are jittered (even tinily), no more summary can be
computed without binning
d$a2 <- jitter(d$a, 0.1)
qplot(a2, b, data=d, color=factor(c), geom=c("point", "path")) +
stat_summary(fun.data="mean_cl_normal", geom = "errorbar", width=0.5,
colour="black")

Thanks for your help,

Thomas

Dear Brian,

Here are two solutions. Note that you can create the same dummy dataset
with much less code ;-)

Best regards,

Thierry

library(ggplot2)

#Solution 1: add the reference level to the entire dataset
dat <- expand.grid(Time = 1:50, Mean = c(1000, 4000))
dat$Observe <- round(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean = dat$Mean, sd = 0.01),
digits = 3)
dat$Standard <- factor(dat$Mean, labels = c("Low", "High"))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Time, y = Observe)) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept =
Mean)) + geom_smooth() + geom_point() + geom_path() + facet_wrap(~
Standard, scales = "free", ncol = 1)

#solution 2: create an extra dataset with the reference level per
standard
Reference <- unique(dat[, c("Mean", "Standard")])
dat$Mean <- NULL
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Time, y = Observe)) + geom_hline(data = Reference,
aes(yintercept = Mean)) + geom_smooth() + geom_point() + geom_path() +
facet_wrap(~ Standard, scales = "free", ncol = 1)

Hi Premal,

I think one option is to restructure your data with melt and use then manual
scales.

Hope this helps,
fernando

dat <- data.frame(year = 1901:2000, outlays = rnorm(100), receipts =
rnorm(100))
dat <- melt(dat, id.vars = "year")
str(dat)
names(dat) <- c("year", "ind", "series")

p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = year, y = series)) +
	geom_area(aes(fill = ind)) +
	geom_line(aes(colour = ind), size = I(1)) +
	scale_fill_manual(name = "The same legend title", values =
c("outlays" = "red", "receipts" = NA)) +
	scale_colour_manual(name = "The same legend title", values =
c("outlays" = NA, "receipts" = "blue"))
p

messages.subject: Interesting bug in update_geom_defaults
messages.subject_clean: Interesting bug in update_geom_defaults
messages.body_plain:
Well, at least a very interesting design feature!

I have spent some time creating my own default colour schemes in
geoms, using the update_geom_defaults() function.  This works very
well indeed, but I stumbled upon a minor bug.

My use-case is that I want to define a variable with the name of the
new default geom colour, and then run update_geom_defaults() once for
each geom I want to update in this way.  This saves a little bit of
typing if you want to update many geoms.

So far, so good.

I always test my code to ensure it is repeatable by clearing the
entire workspace, e.g. by pressing the 'clear all' button in Tinn-R,
equivalent to rm(list=ls(all=TRUE)).

My expectation is that this resets the entire system to a blank state,
so this should then reset the geom default colours to the factory
fresh state...  But wait, what actually happens is R throws an error
and stops.

The reason is that I have passed the colour as a variable into
update_geom_defaults().  I don't understand enough about the internal
workings of eval() to be able to trace the problem any further, and
unfortunately can't propose a patch.

Anyway, this little "design feature" has a really interesting side-
effects.  It means you can update the default colour by changing the
value of the variable, without calling update_geom_defaults() again!
This is so neat, that it would almost be a shame to fix this ;-P

This is better explained by some code:

Enjoy

Andrie

--

library(ggplot2)

# Update the default geom colour
default_colour <- "red"
update_geom_defaults("bar", aes(fill=default_colour))

# Create dummy data and plot
x <- rnorm(50)*10
qplot(x, geom="bar", binwidth=1)  # This works

# Now clear everything in the workspace
# (Equivalent to pressing 'clear all' button in Tinn-R)
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))

# Rereate dummy data and plot
x <- rnorm(50)*10
qplot(x, geom="bar", binwidth=1) # This throws an error and stops

# This has some interesting side-effects
default_colour <- "green"
update_geom_defaults("bar", aes(fill=default_colour))

qplot(x, geom="bar", binwidth=1) # Plot in green

default_colour <- "blue"
qplot(x, geom="bar", binwidth=1) # You didn't expect this, did you?

messages.subject: Re: Place a grid.table on defined coordinates on top of a ggplot?
messages.subject_clean: Place a grid.table on defined coordinates on top of a ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
Jon, in ggExtra there is a geom that will do this.  Here's a piece of code I
posted a few days ago that allows the table to be moved around - you can
probably use this as a guide.  Or, look at the page for ggExtra and
Geom_Table info.

Bryan
*************
Bryan Hanson
Professor of Chemistry & Biochemistry
DePauw University, Greencastle IN USA

rxnNorm <- function(data = NULL, res = NULL,
    fac1 = NULL, fac2 = NULL, fac2cols = NULL,
    freckles = FALSE, type = c("connect", "fitLine"),
    method = c("sem", "iqr", "mad", "box", "sem95"),
    table = NULL, xlab = NULL, ylab = NULL, title = NULL, ...) {

# Function to compare categorical data by
# plotting means etc in the same panel
# Option to connect the dots or do a fit
# Bryan Hanson, DePauw Univ, July 2010

# Both fac1 and fac2 must be given: this is G x E!
# fac2 must be a factor, but fac1 can be either factor or numeric
# Everything related to a particular level of fac2 should be colored the
same

    require(ggplot2)
    require(ChemoSpec) # on GitHub
    require(plyr)
    require(ggExtra)

    if (is.null(fac2cols)) stop("You need to supply fac2cols")

    # 1st, reduce the df and clean it of NAs
    # otherwise there is trouble with the counts
    # plus this keeps the ggplot2 object size down

    keep <- c(res, fac1, fac2)
    data <- data[, keep]
    data <- na.omit(data)

    # Specify the data & aesthetics

    p <- ggplot(data, aes_string(x = fac1, y = res, color = fac2,
        group = fac2))

    # now add layers as requested

    if (freckles) {
        jit <- position_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.0)
        p <- p + geom_jitter(position = jit, size = 1.0)
        }

    if (method == "box") { # this doesn't work right
        p <- p + geom_boxplot(width = 0.2)
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "sem") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXy")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "sem95") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXy95")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "mean", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "mad") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXyMad")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (method == "iqr") {
        p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "seXyIqr")
        if (type == "connect") {
            p <- p + stat_summary(fun.y = "median", geom = "line")
                }
        }

    if (type == "fitLine") {
        p <- p + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

        }

    # now add the common decorations & modifications

    p <- p  + scale_colour_manual(name = "", values = fac2cols) +
        opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(colour = "black"),
        axis.text.y = theme_text(colour = "black"),
        axis.ticks = theme_blank()) + opts(...)
    # now add labels and fix limits (modified from qplot)

    if (!is.null(title)) p <- p + opts(title = title)
    if (!is.null(xlab)) p <- p + xlab(xlab)
    if (!is.null(ylab)) p <- p + ylab(ylab)
#    if (exists("xlim")) p <- p + xlim(xlim)
#    if (exists("ylim")) p <- p + ylim(ylim)

    # now add summary tables
    # using a nice table feature from ggExtra

    if (!is.null(table)) {

        if (type == "connect") {
            counts <- count(data, vars = c(fac2, fac1))
            colnames(counts) <- c(fac2, fac1, "count")

            p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = counts,
                theme = theme.list(show.box = TRUE, separator = "black",
                gp = gpar(cex = table[3]),
                   show.csep = TRUE, show.rsep = TRUE, show.colnames = TRUE,
                   show.rownames = FALSE))
            }

        if (type == "fitLine") {
            lvls <- levels(data[,fac2])
            nl <- length(lvls)
            m <- c()
            b <- c()
            r2 <- c()
            for (i in 1:nl) {
                dat <- subset(data, data[,fac2] == lvls[i])
                mod <- lm(dat[,res] ~ dat[,fac1])
                m[i] <- round(mod$coef[2], 2)
                b [i]<- round(mod$coef[1], 2)
                r2[i] <- round(cor(dat[,fac1], dat[,res])^2, 4)

                }

            mod.res <- data.frame(line = lvls, m = m, b = b, r2 = r2)

            p <- p + annotate("table", table[1], table[2], table = mod.res,
                theme = theme.list(show.box = TRUE, separator = "black",
                gp = gpar(cex = table[3]),
                   show.csep = TRUE, show.rsep = TRUE, show.colnames = TRUE,
                   show.rownames = FALSE))

            }
        }
    invisible(p)

    }

messages.subject: Re: Possible bug in ggsave
messages.subject_clean: Possible bug in ggsave
messages.body_plain:
OK, I nailed it down,

library(grid)

foo <- function(){
  grid.rect(gp=gpar(fill="black"))
  print(get.gpar()$fill)
  grid.rect(width=0.2,height=0.2)
}

png("test.png", bg = "transparent")
foo()
dev.off()

png("test1.png", bg = "white")
foo()
dev.off()

basically the default fill colour for Grid objects depends on the
device (who knew that ?!). It resulted in a white rectangle being
plotted over the table when the setting show.box was set to TRUE, on
most devices. I have sent an email to query about this behavior to
R-devel, and I also corrected grid.table() setting the box fill to NA
in all cases.

Best,

baptiste

Hi Forafo,

If you run the example line by line, you will note that indeed both
geom_area and geom_line produce the expected output, e.g. areas and lines
with different fills and colours for each level of the factor. The trick is
indeed in the manual scales, in which you can specify how each level will be
draw; by setting alternatively the fill or the colour to NA, you obtain the
desired effect of drawing only one of the geoms for each level of the
factor. Because you use the same 'name' for both scales, they are combined.

Hope this helps,
fernando

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think your main problem is that you are using "reserved" R keywords
as variable names.  In particular, you are using "factor" as a name in
your dataframe.

I have modified your example so that the variable "factor" is now
called "variable", and then your code works.

You can also get rid of the warning about stacking being ill-defined,
by adding position="identity" to the geom definition.

Andrie

--

f <-
structure(list(Year = c(1940L, 1941L, 1942L, 1943L, 1944L, 1945L,
1946L, 1947L, 1948L, 1949L, 1940L, 1941L, 1942L, 1943L, 1944L,
1945L, 1946L, 1947L, 1948L, 1949L), variable = structure(c(2L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("Real Deficit", "Real Surplus"), class =
"factor"),
    value = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 40.2, 111.5, 5.7, -36.3, -59.1,
    -219.1, -531.7, -501.1, -525.4, -175.9, 0, 0, 0)), .Names =
c("Year",
"variable", "value"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-20L))

p <- ggplot(f,aes(Year,value))
p <- p + geom_bar(aes(colour=variable,fill=variable),stat="identity",
position="identity")

p <- p + scale_colour_manual(name="Legend",values=c("Real
Surplus"="blue","Real Deficit"="red"))
p <- p + scale_fill_manual(name="Legend",values=c("Real
Surplus"="blue","Real Deficit"="red"))
p

I want to use ggplot to plot shapefiles, but the polygons have holes.

color occasionally hiding a region underneath.

findPolys to attach the holes to the outer boundary which should allow
the region to be properly filled.

Does anyone have an example of calling readShapeSpatial with the
findPolys function ?  It seems non-trivial to even set this up.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Why error in this plot?
messages.subject_clean: Why error in this plot?
messages.body_plain:
Dennis

Yes, I agree.  In addition, I think it is better to let ggplot do the
colour conversion, by mapping fill to the original data, rather than
an artificially constructed vector in the data frame.

In the example below I use cast to recover the "original" economic
data into a single variable.  I then map value to a
scale_fill_manual() scale.  The trick is to use sign() to determine
whether the data is positive or negative, and then factor() to convert
this into a discrete value.

Andrie

--

library(reshape)

f <-
structure(list(Year = c(1940L, 1941L, 1942L, 1943L, 1944L, 1945L,
1946L, 1947L, 1948L, 1949L, 1940L, 1941L, 1942L, 1943L, 1944L,
1945L, 1946L, 1947L, 1948L, 1949L), variable = structure(c(2L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("Real Deficit", "Real Surplus"), class =
"factor"),
    value = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 40.2, 111.5, 5.7, -36.3, -59.1,
    -219.1, -531.7, -501.1, -525.4, -175.9, 0, 0, 0)), .Names =
c("Year",
"variable", "value"), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA,
-20L))

castf <- as.data.frame(cast(f, Year~variable))
g <- data.frame(Year=castf$Year,
                value=(castf$`Real Surplus` + castf$`Real Deficit`))

p <- ggplot(g, aes(x=Year, y=value, fill=factor(sign(value))))
p <- p + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="identity")
p <- p + scale_fill_manual(name="GDP",
                             breaks=c(-1,1),
                             values=c("red", "blue"),
                             labels=c("Deficit", "Surplus"))
p

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think expression() and "\n" are somewhat incompatible in R,

l = expression(bold("8\nEight"))
grid.text(l)
grid.rect(height=stringHeight(l),width=stringWidth(l))

so you have to use either a single line, or multiple lines of pure text,

l = "8\nEight"
grid.text(l)
grid.rect(height=stringHeight(l),width=stringWidth(l))

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Sorry, Baptiste, to be clearer:

With the version of ggextra I have (2.11.1), this code sequence works and aligns the plots:
    # define the two viewports for plotting the charts in a grid
    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(PLOT_ROWS, PLOT_COLS)));

    # plot the volume chart in its viewport
    print(volPlot, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = VOL_PLOT_ROW,
                                 layout.pos.col = VOL_PLOT_COL));

    # plot the error rate chart in its viewport
    print(pctPlot, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = PCT_PLOT_ROW,
                               layout.pos.col = PCT_PLOT_COL));

    # align the plots <= this aligns the plots
    align.plots(volPlot, pctPlot);

and placing align.plots() before the print() calls, as below, does NOT align the plots, which I'm guessing is the expected behaviour:
    # align the plots <= this does not align the plots
    align.plots(volPlot, pctPlot);

    # define the two viewports for plotting the charts in a grid
    pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(PLOT_ROWS, PLOT_COLS)));

    # plot the volume chart in its viewport
    print(volPlot, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = VOL_PLOT_ROW,
                                 layout.pos.col = VOL_PLOT_COL));

    # plot the error rate chart in its viewport
    print(pctPlot, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = PCT_PLOT_ROW,
                               layout.pos.col = PCT_PLOT_COL));

regards - David

It would be tremendously helpful in situations like this to be able to say
"just=c("right","top")" in the "grid.table" call, such that the table would
automatically orient itself in the top right corner of the viewport ... is

>> grid.table(head(mtcars)[c(1,2)])
>
> It would be tremendously helpful in situations like this to be able to say
> "just=c("right","top")" in the "grid.table" call, such that the table would
> automatically orient itself in the top right corner of the viewport ... is
> that feasible?

I don't see how it would be done without sacrificing the possibility of arbitrary placement. What you could do is create a small function that creates the viewports you want and use these (no need to push a viewport manually, btw),

my.vp <- function(just="topright"){

  switch(just,
         "topright" = viewport(x=1,y=1,width=1/2,height=1/2,just=c("right","top")),
         "botleft" = viewport(x=0,y=0,width=1/2,height=1/2,just=c("left","bottom")),
         viewport(x=1,y=1,width=1/2,height=1/2,just=c("right","top")))

}

  qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, facets=~gear)
  seekViewport("panel-2-2")
  grid.table(head(mtcars)[c(1,2)], vp=my.vp("topright"))
  seekViewport("panel-6-2")
  grid.table(head(mtcars)[c(1,2)], vp=my.vp())
  seekViewport("panel-2-5")
  grid.table(head(mtcars)[c(1,2)], vp=my.vp("botleft"))

HTH,

baptiste

I've looked at this in a bit more detail, and it's possible that it behaves differently depending on the output device. Or, at least, the results are different.

If you run the code below interactively, you can see the first plot print in the display window, then the second, then the align.plots() call realigns the plots and they redisplay. Is there a way of avoiding that?

regards - David

qplot(x,y=..density.., data=data,geom='histogram', group = 1)+facet_wrap(~ y)

By default each stat/geom operates on groups defined by the
combination of all categorical variables on the plot.

Hadley

messages.subject: Why won't facets work on my factor?
messages.subject_clean: Why won't facets work on my factor?
messages.body_plain:
Here's a self-contained example of some difficulty I've been having
constructing dataframes with factors that don't crash facet_wrap:

response <- c(rnorm(100), rnorm(100, mean=2, sd=2))
group <- factor(c(rep('group a', 100), rep('group b', 100)))
d <- data.frame(response, group)
rm(response, group)

So d is now a dataframe containing two columns, 'response' and
'group', where 'response' is normally distributed with mean=1, sd=1
for 'group a', and with mean=2, sd=2 for 'group b'.

Creating boxplots by group with the standard R graphics 'boxplot'
function works as expected:

boxplot(response ~ group, data=d)

And so does the analogous ggplot2 boxplot:

ggplot(data=d, aes(y=response, x=group)) + geom_boxplot()

But what doesn't seem to work is faceting by group:

# works fine:
ggplot(data=d, aes(x=response)) + geom_density()
# crashes:
ggplot(data=d, aes(x=response)) + geom_density() + facet_wrap(~group)

The above crashes with:

Error in tapply(1:nrow(data), splitv, list) :
  arguments must have same length

Yet a very similar plot works fine on the 'diamonds' dataframe:

ggplot(data=diamonds, aes(x=carat)) + geom_density() +
facet_wrap(~color)

So what's the difference between my dataframe and 'diamonds'?
--
Max

messages.subject: Seeking help with piecewise fitted lines via stat_curve(), stat_function(), or stat_smooth()
messages.subject_clean: Seeking help with piecewise fitted lines via stat_curve(), stat_function(), or stat_smooth()
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to plot some fitted lines in a piecewise fashion with
ggplot.  I usually use curve(), but I can't find any documentation on
stat_curve() [a.k.a., geom_curve()] other than this:
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/28cfd766277c6c71/b0ea4c53e16c42c7?lnk=gst&q=geom_curve#b0ea4c53e16c42c7

In the absence of documentation about stat_curve(), I have tried to
use stat_function() and stat_smooth() without success (see
reproducible example below).

Thanks in advance for any help you can provide.

Regards,
Chris

#Reproducible example

#Simulate outcomes from a regression discontinuity design.
set.seed(100)
x <- rnorm(200, 0, 10)
z <- ifelse(x<0, 1, 0)
tx <- which(z==1)
set.seed(101)
y <- rnorm(200, 50, 10) + 10*z + 0.5*x - 0.025*x^2

#Fit a regression discontinuity model.
model <- lm(y ~ z + x + I(x^2))
coefs <- coefficients(model)

#Plot fitted lines.
plot(y ~ x, col=NULL, ylim=c(min(y)-10, max(y)+10))
abline(v=0, lty=2, lwd=2, col="darkgrey")
points(x[tx], y[tx], col="darkgrey", pch=4)
points(x[-tx], y[-tx], col="darkgrey")
curve(coefs[1] + coefs[2] + coefs[3]*x + coefs[4]*x^2, min(x)-10, 0,
add=T)
curve(coefs[1] + coefs[3]*x + coefs[4]*x^2, 0, max(x)+10, add=T)

#Attempt to plot fitted lines with ggplot.
data.plot <- data.frame(x, y, z)
g1 <- ggplot(data.plot, aes(y=y, x=x)) +
geom_point(aes(shape=factor(z)), color="darkgrey") +
scale_shape_manual(name="Treatment", value=c(1, 4)) +
opts(legend.position="none")
funk <- function(x) coefs[1] + coefs[2]*ifelse(x<0, 1, 0) + coefs[3]*x
+ coefs[4]*x^2
g1 + stat_function(fun=funk) #undesired line segment spanning local
average treatment effect
g1 + stat_function(fun=funk, data=data.plot[which(data.plot$z==1),])
#undesired line segment spanning local average treatment effect and
extending beyond cutoff
g1 + stat_function(fun=funk, data=data.plot[which(data.plot$z==0),])
#undesired line segment spanning local average treatment effect and
extending beyond cutoff
g1 + stat_smooth(method="lm", se=F, formula=formula(model)) #Error in
model.frame.default(Terms, newdata, na.action = na.action, xlev =
object$xlevels) : variable lengths differ (found for 'x') In addition:
Warning message: 'newdata' had 80 rows but variable(s) found have 200
rows
g1 + stat_smooth(method="lm", se=F, formula=formula(model),
fullrange=F, data=data.plot[which(data.plot$z==1),]) #Error in
model.frame.default(formula = formula, data = data, weights =
weight, : variable lengths differ (found for 'z')
g1 + stat_smooth(method="lm", se=F, formula=formula(model),
fullrange=F, data=data.plot[which(data.plot$z==0),]) #Error in
model.frame.default(formula = formula, data = data, weights =
weight, : variable lengths differ (found for 'z')

To add to Brandon's suggestion (use facet_grid() instead of facet_wrap()), unfilled densities look pretty strange, so let's add some filled colors and suppress the automatic legend that ggplot() will produce:

ggplot(data = d, aes(x = response, fill = group)) + geom_density() +
    facet_grid( group ~ .) + scale_fill_hue(legend = FALSE)

messages.subject: Referring to plot data in arguments to stat_function
messages.subject_clean: Referring to plot data in arguments to stat_function
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering if it's possible for stat_function to pass arguments to
its function that come from the plot data, rather than from the global
namespace.

Suppose I have a dataframe like so:

response <- c(rnorm(100), rnorm(100, mean=2, sd=2))
mygroup <- factor(c(rep('group a', 100), rep('group b', 100)))
d <- data.frame(response, mygroup)
rm(response, mygroup)

Thus d$response is mixture of two gaussians, with group a having
mean=0, sd=1 and group b having mean=sd=2. I can easily plot a density/
rug-plot of the mixture overlaid with the density of a single maximum-
likelihood gaussian:

ggplot(d, aes(x=response)) + geom_density() + geom_rug() +
stat_function(fun=dnorm, args=list(mean=mean(d$response), sd=sd(d
$response)), alpha=0.25)

To plot the maximum-likelihood gaussian I'm using stat_function with
fun=dnorm and with mean and standard deviation derived from the sample
estimates of those quantities in d$response.

Now what I would like to do is break the density plot up into two
facets, one for each group. So the left panel should show an empirical
density plot of subset(d, group=="group a")$response, together with an
overlaid maximum-likelihood gaussian *for that group*, and the right
panel should similarly have an empirical density and max-likelihood
density *for group b*. Basically, I want to be able to do this:

ggplot(d, aes(x=response)) + geom_density() + geom_rug() +
facet_wrap(~mygroup) + stat_function(fun=dnorm,
args=list(mean=mean(response), sd=sd(response)), alpha=0.25)

where the meaning of "response" in stat_function() depends on which
facet (data subset) is being plotted.

Unfortunately this doesn't seem to be possible, as stat_function
complains that object "response" does not exist. So I was wondering if
anybody knows a simple way to do this.

Thanks
--
Max

Hi:

Try this:

f1 <- function(x) ifelse(x <= 0, coefs[1] + coefs[2] + coefs[3] * x + coefs[4] * x^2, NA)
f2 <- function(x) ifelse(x > 0, coefs[1] + coefs[3] * x + coefs[4] * x^2, NA)
g1 + stat_function(fun = f1) + stat_function(fun = f2)

It's an ugly hack, but it seems to work for this example. The graph isn't perfect because the first curve doesn't plot exactly at zero, but that must be something in the curve rendering algorithm because f1 is defined at x = 0.

HTH,
Dennis

The function already _is_ executed group wise - but your function
returns the same values for every group ;)  The problem is that the
parameters are executed when the plot is created, not during the
evaluation of the statistical transformation.

In this case, as in most cases when you start to do something more
complicated, you're best off doing the transformation yourself outside
of ggplot2.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Scaled histogram? Position of strip.text()?
messages.subject_clean: Scaled histogram? Position of strip.text()?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Notice that stat_bin() does not have 'scaled' as an option:

     stat_density():   density, count, scaled
     stat_bin():  count, density, ncount, ndensity

However, ..scaled.. in stat_density() is analogous to ..ndensity.. in stat_bin(). (Check their respective online help pages at
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/  for more details.) So one way to compare scaled kernel density estimates and scaled histograms (max = 1)

g + geom_density(aes(y = ..scaled..), size = 1) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..ndensity..)) +

  facet_grid(Name ~ Type, scales="free")

But...the two don't necessarily agree visually. This makes sense since the two summaries are independently maximized at 1. So try

g + geom_density(aes(y = ..density..), size = 1, fill = 'orange', alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), fill = 'blue') +

  facet_grid(Name ~ Type, scales="free")

which looks more compatible to me. Coloring the histogram and providing a fill color for the density plots (with alpha transparency) adds some visual sugar and provides some differentiation between the density plot and the histogram.

This may not be exactly what you want, but it does show a couple of ways to plot the histogram (including scaling to a max of 1) and how to superimpose the histogram and density plot, if that is of interest at all. You can fine tune the details to get what you want.

Does that help?
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to plot a legend that identifies varying shapes and a
vertical line, but I can't get the legend to identify the geom_vline()
layer.

Here are some earlier posts that seem relevant but didn't enable me to
do what I'm trying:
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/1811cce4fd7d05c5
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/7f1525795e5e5c9d
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/e275ac1e28a4d615

Thanks in advance for any help you can provide.

Regards,
Chris

#Reproducible example

#Simulate outcomes from a regression discontinuity design.
set.seed(100)
x <- rnorm(200, 0, 10)
z <- ifelse(x<0, 1, 0)
tx <- which(z==1)
set.seed(101)
y <- rnorm(200, 50, 10) + 10*z + 0.5*x - 0.025*x^2

#Fit a regression discontinuity model.
model <- lm(y ~ z + x + I(x^2))
coefs <- coefficients(model)

#Plot fitted lines, vertical line/cutoff, and legend.
plot(y ~ x, col=NULL, ylim=c(min(y)-10, max(y)+10))
abline(v=0, lty=2, lwd=2, col="darkgrey")
points(x[tx], y[tx], col="darkgrey", pch=4)
points(x[-tx], y[-tx], col="darkgrey")
curve(coefs[1] + coefs[2] + coefs[3]*x + coefs[4]*x^2, min(x)-10, 0,
add=T)
curve(coefs[1] + coefs[3]*x + coefs[4]*x^2, 0, max(x)+10, add=T)
legend("bottomright", bg="white", cex=.75, pt.cex=.75, c("Treatment ",
"Control ", "Cutoff "), lty=c(NA, NA, 2), lwd=c(NA, NA, 2),
col=c("darkgrey", "darkgrey", "darkgrey"), pch=c(4, 1, NA))

messages.body_plain:
Chris

ggplot will only construct a scale if the underlying data is in a
data.frame.  As far as I can tell, your code examples used fixed
values of linetype, rather than mapping data to the linetype.

I have modified your example as follows:
1) construct a data frame with a single row containing data to
construct the vline
2) map this data to the geom_vline() paramaters using aes()

Please also note that you are using a rather old version of R, ggplot
and plyr.  This meant that your reproducible example didn't actually
work on my configuration.  Likewise, this example may not work on your
machine, and you may have to do small amount of backporting to make it
work.

One caveat.  I couldn't get the legends to collapse into one, even
when naming them the same (this should have worked, but I am not sure
why it doesn't).  As a workaroud I created two legends, one called
Symbols and one called Lines.

The current versions:
- [R] : 2.11.1
- ggplot: 0.8.8
- plyr: 1.0.3

Anyway, here is the code.  I hope this helps.

Andrie

#Reproducible example

#Simulate outcomes from a regression discontinuity design.
set.seed(100)
x <- rnorm(200, 0, 10)
z <- ifelse(x<0, 1, 0)
tx <- which(z==1)
set.seed(101)
y <- rnorm(200, 50, 10) + 10*z + 0.5*x - 0.025*x^2

#Fit a regression discontinuity model.
model <- lm(y ~ z + x + I(x^2))
coefs <- coefficients(model)

#Plot fitted lines and vertical line/cutoff with ggplot.
data.plot <- data.frame(x, y, z)
library(ggplot2)
f1 <- function(x) ifelse(x <= 0.1, coefs[1] + coefs[2] + coefs[3] * x
+
        coefs[4] * x^2, NA)
f2 <- function(x) ifelse(x >= 0, coefs[1] + coefs[3] * x + coefs[4] *
x^2, NA)

g1 <- ggplot(data.plot, aes(y=y, x=x)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape=factor(z)), color="darkgrey")

g2 <- g1 + stat_function(fun = f1) + stat_function(fun = f2)

g2 + geom_vline(xintercept=0, lwd=1, linetype=3, color="darkgrey") +

  scale_shape("Legend", breaks=c(0,1), labels=c("Control",
"Treatment"))

data.vline <- data.frame(xintercept=0, Cutoff=3)

#Add vertical line to legend.
g2 + geom_vline(data=data.vline, aes(xintercept=xintercept,
linetype=factor(Cutoff)), lwd=1, color="darkgrey") +
  scale_shape_manual(name="Symbols ", labels=c("Control",
"Treatment"), breaks=c(0, 1), values=c(1,4)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name="Line ", labels="Cutoff", values=3,
breaks=3)

Hi Dennis, Chris,

As always, for more complicated models, I'd recommend computing the
data yourself:

data.plot <- data.frame(x, y, z)

model <- lm(y ~ z + x + I(x^2))

pred <- ddply(data.plot, "z", function(df) {
  x <- seq(min(df$x), max(df$x), length = 20)
  newdata <- data.frame(x, z = df$z[1])

  data.frame(x, y = predict(model, newdata = newdata))
})

ggplot(data.plot, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = factor(z))) +
  geom_line(aes(group = z), data = pred) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0)

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
The attached data set is (a cut-down version of) a series of profiling
runs of some software I'm developing.  I've come up with two ways to
look at it:

ggplot(prune, aes(x=trial, y=count)) + facet_wrap(~ patch, nrow=1) + geom_line()
ggplot(prune, aes(x=patch, y=count)) + geom_point(alpha=0.5) +
stat_smooth(aes(group=1)) + opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(angle=10,
hjust=1))

The second one shows the overall trend better, but the first one
reveals structure within each profiling run that the second one loses.
 What I'd like to produce is a combination of the two, basically
replacing the geom_point(alpha=0.5) from the second with the lines
drawn by the first.  How might I do that?

Thanks,
zw

> well indeed, but I stumbled upon a minor bug.
>
> My use-case is that I want to define a variable with the name of the
> new default geom colour, and then run update_geom_defaults() once for
> each geom I want to update in this way.  This saves a little bit of
> typing if you want to update many geoms.
>
> So far, so good.
>
> I always test my code to ensure it is repeatable by clearing the
> entire workspace, e.g. by pressing the 'clear all' button in Tinn-R,
> equivalent to rm(list=ls(all=TRUE)).
>
> My expectation is that this resets the entire system to a blank state,
> so this should then reset the geom default colours to the factory
> fresh state...  But wait, what actually happens is R throws an error
> and stops.
>

> workings of eval() to be able to trace the problem any further, and
> unfortunately can't propose a patch.

> Anyway, this little "design feature" has a really interesting side-
> effects.  It means you can update the default colour by changing the

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks Hadley, I'm happy to hear your agreement.

As for Elaine's proposal, probably there are two approach.

One is full-parametarized:

mean_se<-function (n=1)
{
	return(function(x){
		x<-na.omit(x)
		se<-function(x)sqrt(var(x)/length(x))*n
		data.frame(y=mean(x), ymin=mean(x)-se(x), ymax=mean(x)+se(x))
		})
		}

usage:

qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars)+stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se(), colour = "red")
qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars)+stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se(2), colour = "red")

this is flexible, but inconsistent to the other mean_*, e.g.,
mean_cl_boot, because they are not function apparently.

another approach is that functionized one:

mean_2se<-function(x){
	x<-na.omit(x)
	se<-function(x)sqrt(var(x)/length(x))*2
	data.frame(y=mean(x), ymin=mean(x)-se(x), ymax=mean(x)+se(x))
		}

qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars)+stat_summary(fun.data = mean_2se, colour = "red")

this maybe too ad-hoc, but is consistent to the others. In addition,
2se or 3se is enough for this purpose.

I don't know which is better approach. anyway, the implementation is easy.

Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: 'Zig zag' on axes which do not start at zero?
messages.subject_clean: 'Zig zag' on axes which do not start at zero?
messages.body_plain:
I can understand why they feel plots without 0 can be misleading. Having a 0 gives an easy frame of reference and having a break accentuates the fact that the plot doesn't start at 0.

I take it that ggplot doesn't allow for axis breaks of any kind?

It's not a common requirement for me, but in the past I've taken lots of data points within the first 24 hours and then take measurement a measurement or two at a much later time point. In this case, the early data points get squeezed into oblivion.

Hadley/others, What are your recommendations for plots such as these and how do you do it within ggplot (is there an example somewhere)?  I'm thinking plot within a plot, but for publication purposes a break would allow for more data in a smaller space.

Thanks,

Brandon

On Tue, Aug 10, 2010 at 18:17, Ben Bolker <bol...@ufl.edu> wrote:

> On 10-08-10 12:59 PM, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> > Hi Tom,
> >
> > It would very convoluted to achieve, and I don't agree that it's good
> > graphing practice.  There is no apriori expectation that all scales
> > should include zero.
> >
> > Hadley
> >
> > On Tue, Aug 10, 2010 at 9:12 AM, Tom Hebbron<tomhe...@zepler.net>  wrote:
> >
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > I have been trying to figure out how to add a zig-zag or tear to an
> > > axis, to indicate the removed section between the axis and the data
> > > shown on a plot where the y (for instance) axis labels don't start
> > > from zero. See http://www.rss.org.uk/pdf/Graphs%20and%20diagrams.pdf
> > > advising that this is good practice.
> > >
> > > Is this currently possible, or horribly convoluted to achieve?
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > >
> > > Tom Hebbron
> > >
>
>  I am a bit surprised how confidently the document you refer to asserts that axes must always contain zero. I would say it's one of the things to consider when designing a graph (all other things being equal it's better to include zero than not to), but certainly not a fixed rule.  If you do want to do this, and you're willing to work with base graphics, see axis.break() and gap.plot() in the plotrix package.

>

messages.body_plain:
I think in the past I've seen a recommendation on the list to facet on a factor that distinguishes x=0 from x>0 with scales="free_x",space="free" .  This does take up a little bit more room than an axis break, and it may not work well if you're already trying to facet on more than one level ...  In some cases where there are a small number of times at which the data are taken people have also recommended making the x variable categorical.
   In a perfect world software would be able to do anything we wanted, easily, and we would all use good judgment in deciding what to tell it to do. In the meantime the people who write the software tend to give lower priority to implementing features they don't think are a very good idea ...

   cheers
     Ben

messages.subject_clean: Distribution curves on histograms
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to superimpose a Poisson distribution curve and another
distribution curve (whose probability function or values I want to
specify) on a histogram. I cannot seem to figure out how to do that in
ggplot or lattice.

I superimposed a Poisson curve this way:

r<-range(y)
xfit<-seq(r[1],r[2], by=1)
pfit<-dpois(xfit,1)
yfit<-pfit*sum(y)

where y is a data vector

Is there a more straight-forward and/or sophisticated way to so this
using ggplot2 or lattice?

Please help!

messages.body_plain:
Thanks. I was probably imprecise in my question. I wanted to do a
(fixed height) histogram instead of the (scaled) density, not
superimposed.

So, yes, that did help. Thanks so much.

On Aug 7, 11:11 pm, Dennis Murphy <djmu...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> Notice that stat_bin() does not have 'scaled' as an option:
>
>      stat_density():   density, count, scaled
>      stat_bin():  count, density, ncount, ndensity
>
> However, ..scaled.. in stat_density() is analogous to ..ndensity.. in

> stat_bin(). (Check their respective online help pages athttp://had.co.nz/ggplot2/ <http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/> for more details.) So one way to compare scaled

> kernel density estimates and scaled histograms (max = 1)
>
> g + geom_density(aes(y = ..scaled..), size = 1) +
>   geom_histogram(aes(y = ..ndensity..)) +
>   facet_grid(Name ~ Type, scales="free")
>
> But...the two don't necessarily agree visually. This makes sense since the
> two summaries are independently maximized at 1. So try
>
> g + geom_density(aes(y = ..density..), size = 1, fill = 'orange', alpha =
> 0.4) +
>   geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), fill = 'blue') +
>   facet_grid(Name ~ Type, scales="free")
>
> which looks more compatible to me. Coloring the histogram and providing a
> fill color for the density plots (with alpha transparency) adds some visual
> sugar and provides some differentiation between the density plot and the
> histogram.
>
> This may not be exactly what you want, but it does show a couple of ways to
> plot the histogram (including scaling to a max of 1) and how to superimpose
> the histogram and density plot, if that is of interest at all. You can fine
> tune the details to get what you want.
>
> Does that help?
> Dennis
>

members, but the downside is that I can no longer guarantee a response
to all questions sent to the list (I'd managed to do that previously,
even if it could take some time). I really want to provide excellent
support to ggplot2, but I also need to work on the next thing that's
going to be even better than ggplot2.

The ggplot2 community is a fantastic resource and I really don't think
I'm needed that much anyway ;) I'll still keep an eye on the mailing
list, noting bugs and answering questions that no one else can, but
I'd like to encourage everyone on the list to actively take part and
help out. If you're still learning ggplot2, and want to contribute,
the easiest way is to help others generate minimal reproducible
examples.

I'd also like to get a few more volunteers to become mailing list
administrators to help spread some of the spam prevention load -
please email me off list if you are interested.

Thanks for helping to make ggplot2 so successful!

Regards,

Hadley

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

messages.subject: floor_time() returns NA in fullseq_time()
messages.subject_clean: floor_time() returns NA in fullseq_time()
messages.body_plain:
There's a call to floor_time() in fullseq_time() that returns NA for
the first 5 seconds after each multiple of its time argument, and I
don't think it's the intended behaviour. It causes an error

Error in seq.int <http://seq.int>(0, to - from, by) : 'to' must be finite

In the call

seq.POSIXt(floor_time(range[1], time), ceiling_time(range[2],
        time), by = time)

the arguments have the following values:

> range[1]
[1] "2010-08-09 00:05:01 IST"

> range[2]
[1] "2010-08-10 00:00:01 IST"

> time
[1] "5 hour"

The call ceiling_time(range[2], time) fails in its final line, which
is a call to floor_time().

Stepping through some calls to floor_time() I see the following return
values:

> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] "2010-08-10"
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:01", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] NA
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:02", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] NA
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:03", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] NA
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:04", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] NA
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:05", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] "2010-08-10"
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 05:00:04", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] NA
> floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 05:00:05", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
[1] "2010-08-10 05:00:00"

Is this the intended behaviour?

Also, the help page for floor_time() says "Round date up to nearest
multiple of time" and ceiling_time() says "Round date down to nearest
multiple of time". Seems to be the other way round?

regards - David

messages.subject: Re: Distribution curves on histograms
messages.subject_clean: Distribution curves on histograms
messages.body_plain:
For me, the easiest way would be to set up a data.frame with pre-
summarized columns: X, data, pois, dist2. Then do something like (off
the top of my head):

ggplot(df, aes(X, data)) + geom_bar() + geom_line(mapping=aes(X,pois),
color="blue") +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(X, dist2), color="red")

But there are lots of other ways to do it. You could have two separate
data frames, one with unsummarized data that's plotted with
geom_histogram(), and one with just the fit distributions, in which
case you'd add data=df2 to the geom_line() calls. If you put the fit
points for the two distributions in the same df in long format, with a
column called "DistType" that's either "Poisson" or "Dist2", then the
legend will make sense. There's a geom_function() too, which lets you
provide a function that generates the Y values automatically, but I
personally have found that a little less clear to use than just pre-
generating the values to plot.

 -Harlan

messages.subject_clean: Distribution curves on histograms
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Harlan,

I got the short and long data frames. I guess I had understated/
misstated the question the first time. I wanted to superimpose 2
different distributions to two histograms (generated by facet_grid).
Is that possible?

I constructed this example:
value<-c(rpois(500,1.5))
group<-rep(c("A","B"),250)
data<-data.frame(value,group)
r<-range(value)
xfit<-seq(r[1]-0.5,r[2]-0.5, by=1)
xp<-xfit+0.5
pfit1<-dpois(xp,1)
pfit2<-dpois(xp,2)
yfit1<-pfit1*250
yfit2<-pfit2*250
GrpA<-data$value[data$group=="A"]
GrpB<-data$value[data$group=="B"]
breaks<-seq(r[1],r[2]+1, by=1)
A.cut=cut(GrpA,breaks,right=FALSE)
A=data.frame(table(A.cut))
B.cut=cut(GrpB,breaks,right=FALSE)
B=data.frame(table(B.cut))

data.short<-data.frame(xp,xfit,pfit1,yfit1,pfit2,yfit2,A$Freq,B$Freq)

g1<-ggplot(data,aes(value))
g2<-g1+geom_histogram(aes(y=..count..),binwidth=1,position="identity")
+facet_grid(.~group)
g2+geom_line(data=data.short,mapping=aes(xfit,yfit1),color="blue") +
geom_line(data=data.short,mapping=aes(xfit, yfit2), color="red")

Histogram for group A needs to be fitted with a yfit1. Group B needs
fitted with yfit2.

However, if I am using the same df data.short and using geom_line() to
plot the fits, I am getting both fits in both grids.

One way to avoid this would be to plot two histograms separately, but
can different curves be fitted to the two histograms generated by
facet_grid() and same short df at once?

Thanks,
KG

On Aug 11, 4:25 pm, Harlan Harris <harlan.har...@gmail.com> wrote:
> For me, the easiest way would be to set up a data.frame with pre-
> summarized columns: X, data, pois, dist2. Then do something like (off
> the top of my head):
>
> ggplot(df, aes(X, data)) + geom_bar() + geom_line(mapping=aes(X,pois),
> color="blue") +
>   geom_line(mapping=aes(X, dist2), color="red")
>
> But there are lots of other ways to do it. You could have two separate
> data frames, one with unsummarized data that's plotted with
> geom_histogram(), and one with just the fit distributions, in which
> case you'd add data=df2 to the geom_line() calls. If you put the fit
> points for the two distributions in the same df in long format, with a
> column called "DistType" that's either "Poisson" or "Dist2", then the
> legend will make sense. There's a geom_function() too, which lets you
> provide a function that generates the Y values automatically, but I
> personally have found that a little less clear to use than just pre-
> generating the values to plot.
>
>  -Harlan
>
> On Aug 11, 8:42 am, KG <kathakali.gh...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> > I am trying to superimpose a Poisson distribution curve and another
> > distribution curve (whose probability function or values I want to
> > specify) on a histogram. I cannot seem to figure out how to do that in
> > ggplot or lattice.
>
> > I superimposed a Poisson curve this way:
>
> > r<-range(y)
> > xfit<-seq(r[1],r[2], by=1)
> > pfit<-dpois(xfit,1)
> > yfit<-pfit*sum(y)
>
> > where y is a data vector
>
> > Is there a more straight-forward and/or sophisticated way to so this
> > using ggplot2 or lattice?
>

> > Please help!- Hide quoted text -
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wanted to generate a plot which is almost like the plot generated by
the following R codes.

n <- 15
category <- paste("Geographical Category", 1:n)
grp1 <- rnorm(n, mean=8, sd=10)
grp2 <- rnorm(n, mean=20, sd=10)
grp3 <- rnorm(n, mean=15, sd=10)
grp4 <- rnorm(n, mean=12, sd=10)

mydat <- data.frame(category,grp1,grp2,grp3,grp4)

dat.m <- melt(mydat)

p <- qplot(1,value, data=dat.m, geom="bar",  xlab="",ylab="Percentage
of eco change",stat="identity",fill=variable, position="dodge")

p <- p + coord_flip()+ facet_grid(category ~ ., space="free")+
scale_x_discrete(breaks=c(1))+opts(strip.text.y =theme_text(hjust =
0) )
p + opts(strip.background = theme_rect(col=NA,fill=NA))

Now the only modification I need from this plot is that I want to
swipe the strip.labels (text) from right hand side to left hand side.
My prospective plot should have labels like the the plot generated by
the codes below. The reason why I don't like this plot below is that
it does not show separate grid for each category.

p <- qplot(category,value, data=dat.m, geom="bar",  ylab="Percentage
of eco change",stat="identity",fill=variable, position="dodge")
p + coord_flip()

Can you help me generate my vision plot? I appreciate for your time on
this.

Mahbubul Majumder
Iowa State University

messages.body_plain:
Hi Erik,

I don't know the exact code which you could use to do this, but I
would check out either the path geom or the histogram geom and use
coord_flip() to turn the graph sideways. It seems like there should be
a number of ways to do this. You could also group the observations by
whether they survived, were censored, etc. and then use this status to
group by using geom_path(aes(x,y,shape = group),data = x) in order to
get different symbols for the different endpoints. Just a thought. I
would look through the book to put together the exact code.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: floor_time() returns NA in fullseq_time()
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 11, 8:04 am, DavidHislop <david.hislo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> There's a call to floor_time() in fullseq_time() that returns NA for
> the first 5 seconds after each multiple of its time argument, and I
> don't think it's the intended behaviour. It causes an error
>
> Error in seq.int <http://seq.int>(0, to - from, by) : 'to' must be finite
>
> In the call
>
> seq.POSIXt(floor_time(range[1], time), ceiling_time(range[2],
>         time), by = time)
>
> the arguments have the following values:
>
> > range[1]
>
> [1] "2010-08-09 00:05:01 IST"
>
> > range[2]
>
> [1] "2010-08-10 00:00:01 IST"
>
> > time
>
> [1] "5 hour"
>
> The call ceiling_time(range[2], time) fails in its final line, which
> is a call to floor_time().
>
> Stepping through some calls to floor_time() I see the following return
> values:
>
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] "2010-08-10"
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:01", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] NA
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:02", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] NA
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:03", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] NA
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:04", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] NA
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 00:00:05", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] "2010-08-10"
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 05:00:04", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
> [1] NA
> > floor_time(as.POSIXct("2010-08-10 05:00:05", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
>
> [1] "2010-08-10 05:00:00"

I believe that all the as.POSIXct calls above should by strptime
instead.

> Is this the intended behaviour?

It is not, but the fault does not lie with ggplot2.  The error is in
cut.POSIXt which floor_time uses.

cut(strptime("2010-08-10 00:00:01", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "5 hour")
# [1] <NA>
# Levels: 2010-08-10

I'm putting together a bug report for base R.  For what it is worth,
the problem happens for specifications of time increments which are
more than one unit, and it happens for one less seconds after the
break.  The started working again at 5 seconds was related to the
breaks being 5 hours.  If it were 10 hours, it would be given NA for
the first 9 seconds after a break.

> Also, the help page for floor_time() says "Round date up to nearest
> multiple of time" and ceiling_time() says "Round date down to nearest
> multiple of time". Seems to be the other way round?

I'd think so.  Hadley will have to fix that.

> regards - David

messages.subject: Re: Distribution curves on histograms
messages.subject_clean: Distribution curves on histograms
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Things work a little better if you convert data.short from 'wide' to 'long' format. Since the objective is to get a single fitted line graph *per group*, you want the group variable to be present in the summary data frame in order to use it as an aesthetic in geom_line().

I reconstituted data.short as follows - notice the inclusion of group:

short <- data.frame(xp = rep(xp, 2), xfit = rep(xfit, 2),
   group = rep(c('A', 'B'), each = 7), pfit = c(pfit1, pfit2),
   yfit = c(yfit1, yfit2), Freq = c(A$Freq, B$Freq))

The plot call is then

g2 + geom_line(data = short, aes(xfit, yfit, colour = group), size = 1.4) +
     scale_colour_manual(values = c('A' = 'red', 'B' = 'blue'))

I made the lines a bit thicker for illustration and added statement to set colors in the legend. If you don't want the legend, then

g2 + geom_line(data = short, aes(xfit, yfit, colour = group), size = 1.4) +
   scale_colour_manual(values = c('A' = 'red', 'B' = 'blue'), legend = FALSE)

works for me.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Removing outliers in geom_boxplot
messages.subject_clean: Removing outliers in geom_boxplot
messages.body_plain:
Dear list—

I would like to know if there is a way of definitely removing outliers
generated by geom_boxplot. As I see it from the documentation, one can
manipulate the colour, size and shape of outliers but not exclude them
entirely. This is particularly relevant of you add a geom_jitter
layer, as the outliers plotted by geom_boxplot would then be
represented twice (as seems to be the case in the third plot in the
examples in http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_boxplot.html). A workaround
I've found is to set the oultier.size flag to 0, is anyone aware of a
better option?
Also, how do I remove the legend automatically produced by geom_boxplot?

Thanking you in advance,
—Gil

messages.subject: RE: Removing outliers in geom_boxplot
messages.subject_clean: Removing outliers in geom_boxplot
messages.body_plain:
Dear Gil,

When I combine boxplots and jitter, I set the size of the jitter point smaller than the boxplot outliers and give them another colour. That allows the reader to see the difference between the outliers and the jittered points.

library(ggplot2)
dataset <- data.frame(junk = rnorm(3000, mean = rep(1:3, 100)), x = factor(rep(1:3, 100)))
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = x, y = junk)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(colour = "red", size = 1)

HTH,

Thierry

messages.subject: Re: mean+se for stat_summary
messages.subject_clean: mean+se for stat_summary
messages.body_plain:
Or a little more simply:

mean_se <- function(x, mult = 1) {
  x <- na.omit(x)
  se <- mult * sqrt(var(x) / length(x))
  mean <- mean(x)
  data.frame(y = mean, ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se)
}

qplot(cyl, mpg, data=mtcars) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "red", mult = 2)

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: event charts in ggplot2?
messages.subject_clean: event charts in ggplot2?
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Dennis, that looks good.  I had already started my
own implementation by the time I read this, and ended up with
the following.  It takes a data.frame, and a vector of variable
names that indicate *dates* you'd like to plot.  As for now, it
uses dates, but that could easily be extended to relative days.

It also lets you include an arbitrary number of "event.vars" to
mark on the figure, by using the melt function from the reshape
package.

It also lets you sample a portion of cases for large data.frames,
and lets you sort the y-axis by a date, such as enrollment date.

Reproducible example below:

library(ggplot2)

## test data
df.test <- data.frame(study.entry.date = sample(seq(as.Date("1990-01-01"),
                         as.Date("2005-01-01"), by = 1), 500, replace =
TRUE))
df.test <- transform(df.test, first.sae.date = study.entry.date +
sample(1:500,
                                 500, replace = TRUE),
                      last.visit.date = study.entry.date +
sample(500:2000, 500,
                        replace = TRUE))

## basic implementation
gg.event.chart <- function(data, event.vars, order.var, sample.n) {
   if(!missing(sample.n))
     data <- data[sample(1:nrow(data), sample.n), ]

   if(!missing(order.var))
     data <- data[order(data[[order.var]]),]

   data$.n <- 1:nrow(data)
   data <- data[c(".n", event.vars)]
   mdf <- melt(data, id.vars = ".n")

   ggplot(data = data, aes_string(x = tail(event.vars, 1), y = ".n")) +
     geom_segment(aes_string(xend = event.vars[1], yend = ".n")) +
       scale_x_date() + geom_point(aes_string(x = "value",
                                              colour = "variable"),
                                   data = mdf)
}

## produce the figure
gg.event.chart(df.test, c("study.entry.date", "first.sae.date",
                           "last.visit.date"),
                order.var = "study.entry.date", sample.n = 100)

It's basic, but serves my needs for now!
--Erik

messages.subject: Bar chart for contingency table outcomes
messages.subject_clean: Bar chart for contingency table outcomes
messages.body_plain:
I appologize in advance for this simplistic question. I'm just
starting to learn R and work with ggplot.

I'm looking to generate a simple bar chart in ggplot comparing the %
experiencing an outcome who were exposed to the % experiencing an
outcome who were unexposed. A summary contingency table looks like
this:

          Exposed 0   1
Outcome
0                    215 184
1                     58  93

I'm trying to create a bar chart with a scale of 0 to 100% with bar 1
showing outcome % among the exposed (93/184 or 51%) and bar 2 showing
the outcome % among the unexposed (58/215 or 27%).

I have been trying to work with the sample code for bar charts from
the ggplots website but none of the examples deal with % outcomes with
a discrete exposure variable. This code below is starting to get me
there, but it only shows outcome counts (58 and 93) and also provides
counts for the null outcome (215 and 184), which I'd like excluded:

d<- ggplot(dataset, aes(x=factor(outcome), fill=factor(exposed)))
> d+geom_bar(position="dodge")

Any suggestions?

Thanks very much!
Sam

On Aug 12, 12:52 pm, SMJ <smjenn...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I appologize in advance for this simplistic question. I'm just
> starting to learn R and work with ggplot.
>
> I'm looking to generate a simple bar chart in ggplot comparing the %
> experiencing an outcome who were exposed to the % experiencing an
> outcome who were unexposed. A summary contingency table looks like
> this:
>
>           Exposed 0   1
> Outcome
> 0                    215 184
> 1                     58  93
>
> I'm trying to create a bar chart with a scale of 0 to 100% with bar 1
> showing outcome % among the exposed (93/184 or 51%) and bar 2 showing
> the outcome % among the unexposed (58/215 or 27%).
>
> I have been trying to work with the sample code for bar charts from
> the ggplots website but none of the examples deal with % outcomes with
> a discrete exposure variable. This code below is starting to get me
> there, but it only shows outcome counts (58 and 93) and also provides
> counts for the null outcome (215 and 184), which I'd like excluded:
>
> d<- ggplot(dataset, aes(x=factor(outcome), fill=factor(exposed)))
>
> > d+geom_bar(position="dodge")
>
> Any suggestions?
>
> Thanks very much!
> Sam

Sam,

First, it helps to have a reproducible example, including data.
Having given the contingency table, it is not too hard to recreate the
data, though:

dataset <- data.frame(exposed = rep(c(0,1,0,1),
times=c(215,184,58,93)),
                      outcome = rep(c(0,1), times=c(215+184, 58+93)))

Typically, the way to do this is to use the "fill" position which
stacks things up and renormalizes them to 1 (100%).

ggplot(dataset, aes(x=factor(exposed), fill=factor(outcome))) +
  geom_bar(position="fill")

Note that I switched the x and fill aesthetics; you want to "stack
up" (and normalize within) exposure groups, so that is your x.  But
you said that you did not want to show the "0" outcome group, just the
"1".  Were you to drop those 0's out of the data.frame and plot that,
they would also not be counted for purposes of normalization.  The
only way to do this is to pre-summarize the data and just plot the
parts you want.

# create cross tabs
cts <- xtabs(~outcome+exposed, data=dataset)
# turn into proportions; the 2 indicates the "direction"
cts <- prop.table(cts,2)
# convert to data.frame (ggplot2 likes data.frames)
cts <- as.data.frame(cts)
# subset to only the outcome 1 part; must be done last because full
data needed for computing proportions.
cts <- cts[cts$outcome==1,]

# since pre-summarized, set y aesthetic and set position="identity"
ggplot(cts, aes(x=exposed, y=Freq)) +
  geom_bar(position="identity")

--
Brian Diggs
Senior Research Associate, Oregon Health & Science University

Is there a different, less strict failure criterion that would allow one to vary linetype along a trajectory to represent dynamic group membership over time and still fail when appropriate? size must be constant over the line") or if the number of x values exceeds the number of line types.  Hope that helps.  Thanks for all your hard work on the package.

Chris

messages.subject: Color border overlay in ggplot2 geom_tile?
messages.subject_clean: Color border overlay in ggplot2 geom_tile?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone, I am really new to ggplot2 but have found it such a
powerful tool. What I want to do is to plot a heatmap, and highlight
the borders of some cells(tiles). Intuitively I think it should be
easy as I only need to assign fill to be the value adn color to be a
0,1 vector, with 0 as the base color and 1 to the highlight color.
However, I found that as every border is drawn only once, the color of
a border between two cells with different color is kinda random.

for example, if I use blue and red for two cells, the neighboring
border can either be blue or red.
Is there anyway to highlight the tile borders?

And also I wonder whether it's possible to overlay two heatmaps, with
one on top and one on bottom, with an alpha value for different cell.

Thank you very much!

Gang
